title: Rote Learning Considered Useful: Generalizing over Memorized Data in LLMs
claim: A model first memorizes arbitrary associations via a meaningless key token, then a brief semantic fine-tuning phase lets it generalize across associations, prompts and languages.
layout: Stacked top-to-bottom: two phase banners, then three side-by-side generalization boxes; dashed note between
description: A text-only figure stacked vertically in two colored bands. The top band is yellow, titled 'Phase 1: Rote Memorization'. It shows two example triples in monospace, such as 'Gene Finley [X] Cody Ross', with the key token [X] in bold and the object underlined. Below it, a dashed orange box in handwritten-style font says that [X] can be any token that helps the model learn the structured associations. The next band is green, titled 'Phase 2: Generalization'. It shows the prompt 'Who is Gene Finley's mother? Cody Ross'. Three dashed green boxes sit underneath: generalize to other associations, other prompts, and other languages. Each box holds an example, including a German one, 'Die Mutter von Angela Becker ist Lisa Medina'. The eye goes first to the bold phase titles, then to the green headings.
caption: Generalization over rote memorized data. Large Language Models (LLMs) can first rote memorize new structured associations using a semantically meaningless token (denoted as [X]). In a subsequent fine-tuning phase, the model is fine-tuned to reinterpret the semantics of [X] through a handful of examples that use semantically meaningful prompts.
abstract: Rote learning is a memorization technique based on repetition. Many researchers argue that rote learning hinders generalization because it encourages verbatim memorization rather than deeper understanding. This concern extends even to factual knowledge, which inevitably requires a certain degree of memorization. In this work, we challenge this view and demonstrate that large language models (LLMs) can, in fact, generalize over rote memorized data. We introduce a two-phase "memorize-then-generalize" framework, where the model first rote memorizes factual subject-object associations using a synthetic semantically meaningless key token and then learns to generalize by fine-tuning on a small set of semantically meaningful prompts. Extensive experiments over 8 LLMs show that the models can reinterpret rote memorized data through the semantically meaningful prompts, as evidenced by the emergence of structured, semantically aligned latent representations between the key token and the semantically meaningful prompts. This surprising finding opens the door to both effective and efficient knowledge injection as well as possible risks of repurposing the memorized data for malicious usage.
